title: DexNDM: Bridging the Sim-to-Real Gap for Hand Rotation
one_liner: A robotic hand learns to rotate any object by training a tiny model for each finger joint that predicts how that joint alone will move, letting simulation policies work on real hands.
lead: A robot hand trained to rotate objects in a video game often fails on a real hand, because the game simplified how fingers touch things. DexNDM builds a small predictor for each finger joint that corrects the game's predictions using just a few real-world finger movements, so the same learned policy works on diverse real objects.

problem.h2: Why robots fail to rotate real objects
paras: A robot hand trained in simulation to rotate an object learns a strategy: 'when the object tilts this way, move fingers in that pattern.' But a real hand touches things differently than the game predicts. The fingers slip, the object shifts slightly, and the contact forces are unpredictable. What works perfectly in video games fails on real hardware.

A beginner might try to make the simulation more realistic by adding more friction models and contact rules to the game. But that makes the game so complex and computationally slow that training takes forever. And even then, no video-game model perfectly matches the real world, so the trained policy still fails.

callout.b: The core problem in one sentence.
callout.html: Simulation predicts finger movement inaccurately, so policies trained in simulation do not work when applied to real hands.

steps.text: Robot arm moves fingers automatically, recording how each joint truly moves.
For each finger joint, train a small model: 'When simulation says move X, real finger actually moves Y.'
Model learns each joint's unique behavior — friction, slip, contact stiffness — from its own data alone.
When rotating an object, each joint predictor adjusts the simulation's command before sending to the real joint.
Same predictors work on different objects, wrist angles, sizes because each joint's model is independent and captures general slip patterns.

paras: Instead of fixing the simulation's physics model, DexNDM adds a thin corrector layer: for each finger joint, a tiny neural network that maps 'what simulation predicted' to 'what the real joint will actually do.' This is independent per joint, so a joint learns only from its own motion history, not the whole hand at once.

hidden.name: Per-joint prediction error
paras: The hidden quantity is how much each finger joint's actual motion differs from what the simulator predicted. For example, if simulation says 'joint 1 will move 45 degrees' but it actually moves 38 degrees, the error is 7 degrees. The paper's model learns these error patterns for each joint separately.

DexNDM measures this by recording real finger movements with minimal data (from autonomous collection) and comparing them to simulation's predictions. Each joint predictor is trained to minimize the gap between what it guesses and what really happens, learning the unique slip, friction, and contact effects of that single joint.

heat.caption: Darker means larger prediction error; joints that slip or have contact noise are darker (corrector learns them most).

reads.html: Each joint's predictor learns a simple pattern: 'When the game says move this much, the real joint moves that much instead.' Dark cells are joints that slip or change behavior a lot — the prediction error is larger for these joints because they are harder to predict, so the corrector works harder on them.

Joint-wise factorization of dynamics reduces dimensionality (each model is small) and uses data efficiently — a single joint's predictor generalizes across different object shapes because it captures friction and contact mechanics invariant to what is being rotated.

mechanism.h2: Why learning one joint at a time fixes the reality gap
paras: Simulation assumes physics rules like friction and contact that do not exist in reality. When a finger touches a hard object, the contact force can be much larger than the game predicted, causing the joint to move less. When sliding, friction creates unexpected damping. A single neural network trying to predict the whole hand's motion at once would need to model all these effects together, requiring huge amounts of real data and a large model.

DexNDM splits the problem: each joint learns only its own error pattern. This is simpler because each joint sees only its own motion history, not the global hand state. A joint learns that 'when I am supposed to move this much and I am touching something, I slip by this percentage' — a simple local rule. Since each rule is small and local, it only needs a few real finger movements (efficient data use), and the learned patterns transfer across objects because slip and friction are properties of the joint itself, not the specific object.

In operation, the simulation sends each joint its predicted command, the corrector predicts how much that joint will really move, and the policy uses the corrected output to decide the next move. This closes the loop between sim and real: the policy still works, but now it is reading from reality instead of wishful thinking.

stages.s: Simulation predicts each joint should move X
Joint predictor estimates real movement will be Y
Policy sees Y, decides next action based on reality
Real hand executes corrected action, rotates object

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Real scenario: simulator predicts joint 1 should move to 45 degrees, joint is currently at 20 degrees.
Joint 1 corrector inputs: (45, 20) — the predicted angle and current state.
Corrector outputs: 38 degrees (learned that friction reduces movement by 7 degrees in this range).
Policy uses 38, not 45, so it is not surprised when the object does not rotate as much.
Another scenario: same joint at 60 degrees, simulator predicts 75 degrees.
Corrector outputs: 71 degrees (learned slip is smaller at high angles).
Each joint has its own f_i, so a pinky corrector learns different slip than a thumb corrector.

math.note: Each joint's small network learns the relationship between what the simulator thinks will happen and what really happens, captured as a simple input-output mapping.

items.html: Each hand has different finger shapes and sizes, different friction on its palm. If you train the correctors on Hand A and test on Hand B, the learned slip patterns will not match. The correctors must be retrained for a new hand.

If the object is deformable or breaks during rotation, the contact forces change unexpectedly. The correctors learned from rigid objects will mispredicts, because they learned 'this contact force means this slip', but the deformable object has different forces.
If the autonomous data collection does not cover enough different finger positions or contact scenarios, the correctors learn incomplete patterns and miss edge cases where they would be most useful.
Collect real data across a range of joint angles, contact forces, and motion speeds. Each corrector then learns the full friction surface for its joint, not just the narrow slice it happened to see.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Start with a simulation-trained policy that fails on real objects (e.g., a cube rolls off the hand or does not rotate). Collect 20-50 real finger movements via teleoperation or autonomous exploration. Train one small neural network per joint (3 lines of PyTorch per joint). Run the same policy again using corrected predictions. Measure success: does the real hand now rotate the cube, a small toy, and a complex-shaped object without retraining the policy itself?
demo.closing: The demo must show that one hand policy, combined with per-joint correctors trained on minimal real data, rotates objects it has never seen before.
